review_scope: Targeted full-text methods/results review; not exhaustive numeric/supplement extraction
methods: Reservoir simulations compare vertical/horizontal wells and fracture configurations in an Illinois-basin storage/seal model based on FutureGen characterisation. Geometry, permeability/fracture scenarios and pressure-limited injection determine stored mass and plume/trapping behaviour.
findings: Table2 shows configuration-dependent cumulative injection and end-of-injection rates: the vertical case13.14Mt/0.68Mt/y versus a6k horizontal case17.54Mt/0.85Mt/y. Fractures can improve access but expand plume extent and possible interaction with conductive pathways; post-injection trapping mechanisms must be assessed separately.
transfer_limits: Simulated fractures are not a universal injectivity uplift or approved operating method. End rates and cumulative totals cannot recover an unreported annual curve. Increased storage must be assessed with sealing, fracture propagation, drilling and operating burdens, not only tonnes injected.

methods: Comparative legal/governance analysis of EU and China offshore CCS uses doctrinal and discourse analysis through the Collingridge-dilemma lens. It examines binding rules, policy architecture, technology maturity, environmental safeguards and cross-sector coordination.
findings: The study contrasts governance pathways rather than supplying a quantified causal deployment model. It proposes adaptive permitting, coordination and economic-incentive mechanisms and identifies unresolved liability, legitimacy and cross-border fragmentation questions.
transfer_limits: Policy statements and proposed governance instruments do not establish current authorisation for a named route. London-Protocol developments require jurisdiction/project-specific checks; the review does not allocate capacity or validate physical retention. No permitting delay, probability or emissions factor is inferred.

review_scope: Targeted full-text methods/results review; not exhaustive numeric/supplement extraction
methods: Three-layer energy-law framework compares international, national and local/permitting issues across four European CO2 transport development scenarios. It combines legal assessment with stakeholder engagement and distinguishes cross-border instruments, domestic regulation and local approvals.
findings: The2017 legal matrix identifies different barriers for Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands, UK and Norway. Commercial readiness requires available CO2, legal pathways, supportive parties, storage access and a viable business plan; these are separate conditions, not substitutes for one another.
transfer_limits: The historical status matrix is not current legal advice or evidence of2026 route approval. Qualitative legal rankings are not quantified commissioning dates, delay distributions or contracted annual storage service. Current treaties, permissions and operator contracts must be verified independently.

review_scope: Targeted full-text methods/results review; not exhaustive numeric/supplement extraction
methods: Genetic-algorithm well-placement optimisation compares a reservoir simulator with ANN proxies and a proxy retrained using new simulator evaluations. The Pohang model tests injector/producer combinations and CO2 breakthrough; offline and online-updated proxy strategies are explicitly compared.
findings: Table3.3 shows an offline proxy predicting11.38% improvement while full-physics reevaluation gives3.19%. Updating the proxy reduces disagreement between predicted and simulator-evaluated improvements. This directly supports evaluating a coarse-model selected decision under the more detailed model.
transfer_limits: Full-physics validation here is model-to-model, not field validation or proof of global optimality. Cumulative quantities are reported in10^8m3 with their source basis; they are not converted to tonnes without state/composition. The proxy training domain and well-layout constraints cannot be transferred as universal injectivity.

review_scope: Targeted full-text methods/results review; not exhaustive numeric/supplement extraction
methods: Scottish industrial-cluster feasibility/cost study combines2014 point-source emissions, estimated technically capturable fractions, feeder connections and potential reuse of existing gas pipelines. findings: Table2 distinguishes5.68Mt/y emitted from4.19Mt/y estimated capture, with site-specific assumed fractions. Existing Feeder10 nominal unboosted3.5Mt/y and theoretical10Mt/y gas-phase capacities imply different infrastructure needs. Feeder8 availability is expressly unconfirmed.

review_scope: Targeted full-text methods/results review; not exhaustive numeric/supplement extraction
methods: Marine-CCS review covers CO2 phase/heat-transfer behaviour, liquefaction cycles, transport concepts, BOG recovery and integrated vessel control. It compares cold-energy, ammonia/refrigerant and other integrated options and distinguishes simulation studies from shipboard evidence.
findings: The synthesis identifies coupled propulsion/reliquefaction/auxiliary modelling, standardised specific-energy boundaries and long-term sea trials as unresolved needs. Claimed benefits depend on ambient conditions, pressure, fuel-side cooling availability and impurities; many proposed controls remain simulation-based.
transfer_limits: Secondary cross-study percentage savings are not directly comparable to primary matched-feed cases. LNG/ammonia cold-energy benefits cannot be transferred to a distillate-only ship with no such integration. The review supplies neither actual voyage duty nor validated wave/operating limits for our design.

review_scope: Targeted full-text methods/results review; not exhaustive numeric/supplement extraction
methods: Life-cycle shipping model explores interconnected LPG/CO2 cargo systems with four boundary conventions. Vessel engine work, lifetime utilisation, construction and operation feed emissions/cost calculations. One boundary treats both materials as cargo; another includes downstream LPG carbon/source and CO2 sink effects.
findings: The reported combined-cargo shipping factor0.048tCO2/t-cargo has a different denominator/boundary from stored-source CO2. The CO2-only example reports0.67Mt emissions and7.43Mt transported over its lifetime. Changing financial discount rates changes costs/profit but leaves physical transported/emitted quantities unchanged.
transfer_limits: A multi-cargo factor cannot be inserted as a per-tonne-stored or universal international CO2 factor. Tanker operating-cost proxies and country electricity assumptions remain source-specific. Cargo carbon must not be reclassified as independent transport emissions or avoided source emissions without a matched counterfactual.

review_scope: Targeted full-text methods/results review; not exhaustive numeric/supplement extraction
methods: Whole-chain financial comparison uses discounted NPV and real-options analysis for coal-plant capture, ship/offshore-pipeline transport and storage. Options include capture shutdown, abandonment and switching reservoir under uncertain prices, utilisation and storage volumes. Continuous liquefaction and batch shipping require temporary storage.
findings: Flexible decisions can change project value and ship-versus-pipeline investment decisions. The financial model is compared with literature cost cases and shows why matching electricity/fuel assumptions changes reported levelised transport costs. Reservoir exhaustion and abandonment probabilities are conditional model outputs.
transfer_limits: Option values and financial scenario probabilities are not measured maritime reliability, pressure-limited injection or a lifecycle climate optimum. Historical2010-price component assumptions and20–40% flashed-gas recirculation descriptions do not imply atmospheric vent losses. Storage access and energy-state compatibility still need separate evidence.

review_scope: Targeted full-text methods/results review; not exhaustive numeric/supplement extraction
methods: Nordic transport study compares ship and pipeline costs across volumes/distances, selected source hubs and alternative storage sites with different injectivity. It examines ramp-up, pipeline underutilisation and cluster scale using historical regional source inventories.
findings: For a500km/10Mtpa pipeline example,25% utilisation for the first ten years increases specific cost from8.4 to16.1EUR/t versus immediate full utilisation. More injective distant sinks and flexible shipping can be financially attractive; outcomes depend on network/cost assumptions and buildup of connected volumes.
transfer_limits: These are cost and scenario comparisons, not whole-chain climate rankings. Early utilisation does not determine ship fuel intensity or weather availability. Historical sources and candidate sites do not establish current capture contracts or injection access; no economic break-even distance becomes a carbon break-even distance.

review_scope: Targeted full-text methods/results review; not exhaustive numeric/supplement extraction
methods: Two-stage stochastic CCS deployment framework compares expected cost with variability, probabilistic financial risk and downside-risk metrics. Discrete capture/network decisions couple scenarios, while epsilon constraints trace economic-versus-risk tradeoffs for uncertain carbon-tax conditions.
findings: Risk-metric selection changes the types of costly scenarios penalised and the resulting design. Threshold-dependent probabilistic/downside criteria reflect decision-maker preferences; computational difficulty differs with binary risk indicators. The study motivates explicit risk definitions rather than an undefined generic uncertainty score.
transfer_limits: Financial scenario probabilities/subjective thresholds are not empirical failure probabilities, uncertain physical injectivity distributions or a probability of climate benefit. This is prior art for risk-aware planning, not site calibration or a complete lifecycle comparison. No distribution is imported into Paper1.

review_scope: Targeted full-text methods/results review; not exhaustive numeric/supplement extraction
methods: SimCCS combines least-cost geographic candidate-network generation with a MILP for source/reservoir opening, discrete pipeline sizes and flow conservation. Source/sink bounds and a system-wide capture target are linked in one atemporal infrastructure decision.
findings: The California demonstration uses37 major sources and14 oil-field reservoirs. Aggregation creates cost economies, but the paper explicitly states pipeline construction costs were artificially reduced to emphasise network capabilities. It also states the2009 model is atemporal and each target is reoptimised from scratch.
transfer_limits: Low transport cost is not a transferable realistic price or GHG factor. Approximate radial-injectivity/property formulas have stated domains and do not resolve time-dependent pressure fronts. Original site data/code are needed for exact case reproduction; later dynamic SimCCS versions are not the same original model.

review_scope: Targeted full-text methods/results review; not exhaustive numeric/supplement extraction
methods: Europe-wide economic MILP designs capture at steel/cement/refinery sources, pipeline/ship routes and onshore/offshore storage. Country-specific versus collective European capture targets and storage restrictions are compared; sector-specific capture and multimodal costs enter the supply-chain objective.
findings: Offshore-only scenarios require more expensive transport and injection despite similar capture cost. Country-level and Europe-wide targets can change which sources capture CO2, not merely their destination. The paper highlights transnational cooperation requirements alongside economic savings.
transfer_limits: Cost-optimal source selection changes composition, so it is not a matched-source climate comparison. Representing all CCS stages economically does not provide complete lifecycle GHG. Ship-unit-cost sensitivity and projected fleets do not validate operational schedules, pressure-constrained annual service or actual cross-border access.
